He is seeking a regular physical examination as well as a consultation regarding dizziness and headaches he experienced the last time he ascended a mountain. These symptoms eventually went away after his team camped in the same location for an extra day. He is otherwise healthy, and his examination is completely unremarkable. The patient has no past medical history of concern. Which of the following is the best recommendation to avoid or prevent these symptoms?

options.label: A

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Acetazolamide: The most appropriate preventive measure for acute mountain sickness for this patient is acetazolamide. Acute mountain sickness (AMS) generally occurs at >2500 meters; however, it has been reported at lower altitudes. AMS is a syndrome of nonspecific manifestations that can develop within 6-12 hours. Patients experience headaches, dizziness, fatigue, and/or nausea with little to no physical exam findings. The most prominent risk factors for developing altitude illness are a history of altitude illness and the rate of ascent. Why this occurs is still unknown, but MR studies suggest that vasogenic cerebral edema is a component of high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE), which is on a spectrum with AMS. The prevention and treatment of AMS include a gradual ascent allowing acclimation, which is how this patient had a resolution of his symptoms on his prior climb. There is thought to be individual variation, but a graded ascent of at most 400 meters above 3000 meters is recommended. Another measure that is thought to be protective is exposure to high altitudes within 2 months of the intended climb, which may lower rates of AMS by 50%. Hydration is important in preventing dehydration secondary to insensible losses (sweating hyperventilation). In regards to pharmacological prevention of AMS, acetazolamide is the drug of choice. Acetazolamide inhibits renal carbonic anhydrase, causing bicarbonate diuresis with subsequent metabolic acidosis and hyperventilation with a relative risk reduction of 48% vs. placebo. However, any indication of high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE) or high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE), which are more severe forms of altitude illness, would require immediate descent due to the potential life-threatening nature of these conditions. Option C - Ginkgo biloba: Ginkgo biloba has not been shown to be effective in the prevention of acute mountain sickness (AMS). The most effective pharmacological prevention for AMS is acetazolamide. questions.solution: Correct Option A - 31-38%: It is important to use a scientific approach in deciding the timing of extubation after mechanical ventilation in an ICU. Spontaneous breathing trial can be achieved either using a T-piece or a ventilator. If using a ventilator, use a pressure support (PS) of 5-10cm H 2 O with no PEEP, a PEEP of 5cm H 2 O, or a PEEP of 5cm H 2 O only. There is no agreement on the acceptable duration of spontaneous breathing trial, but 30 minutes is accepted as sufficient. As she was pulled out, a strong smell of fumes was noticed. The paramedics noticed agitation and intubated her in the field. Her temperature is 98.0°F, pulse is 88/min, and BP is 121/86 mm of Hg. A co-oximeter measured carboxyhemoglobin (CO-Hb) level is 26%, and hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) therapy is considered. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Lactate: CO-Hgb levels are likely positively correlated with initial lactate levels in carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning. Patients who received HBO treatment had elevated plasma lactate concentrations and additionally had more frequent altered mental status. Although HBO therapy is used in different settings, generally accepted indications for HBO treatment are the presence of significantly increased COHb values and neurologic or cardiac deterioration. However, a lactate value >1.85mmol/L can predict the need for HBO treatment, which could be taken as a measure of severe poisoning. Lactate levels are also increased in alcohol intoxication, salicylate poisoning, and paraquat poisoning. Incorrect Options: Option B - Carboxyhemoglobin (CO-Hgb): While carboxyhemoglobin levels are measured to confirm carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning and guide treatment decisions, it is not considered a marker of the severity of poisoning. CO-Hgb levels indicate the percentage of hemoglobin that is bound to carbon monoxide instead of oxygen. A high CO-Hgb level, as in this case (26%), confirms the diagnosis of CO poisoning, but it does not provide information about the severity of the poisoning or the degree of tissue hypoxia. The severity of CO poisoning is better assessed by clinical features, such as the patient's mental status, oxygen saturation, and the presence of symptoms like confusion, agitation, or altered consciousness. Option C - Creatinine: Creatinine levels are not used as a marker of severity in carbon monoxide poisoning. Creatinine is a waste product produced by muscles and excreted by the kidneys. It is commonly measured to assess kidney function and to estimate glomerular filtration rate (GFR). In cases of carbon monoxide poisoning, the focus is on assessing the extent of tissue hypoxia and damage caused by the lack of oxygen, rather than kidney function. Option D - Creatine phosphokinase (CrPK or CPK): Creatine phosphokinase (also known as creatine kinase or CPK) is an enzyme found in various tissues, including muscle and brain cells. Elevated CPK levels can indicate muscle damage, such as in muscle injuries, heart attacks, or rhabdomyolysis. However, CPK levels are not used as a marker of severity in carbon monoxide poisoning. questions.solution: Correct Option C - Staphylococcus aureus: This patient has a classic presentation of infective endocarditis. While the most common location of cardiac valvular involvement in the left heart, in intravenous (IV) drug users, the tricuspid valve is usually affected due to bacterial seeding from venous blood returning to the right heart. A fever and an associated new cardiac murmur are the most common signs of infective endocarditis. It is given for at least 15-20 hours per day to increase the PaO 2 to at least 60 mmHg or SaO 2 to at least 90%. For patients whose oxygen saturation decreases on exercise and improvement in exercise capacity and shortness of breath with oxygen, ambulatory oxygen therapy should be given to maintain SaO 2 above 90%. Incorrect Options: Option B - Bronchodilators Bronchodilators are the mainstay of treatment with COPD; however, they improve the symptoms and reduce breathlessness. It is the second most common hospital-acquired infection and the leading cause of hospital-acquired infection-associated death. The at-risk patients include the elderly, admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU), and mechanically ventilated (ventilator-associated pneumonia). The organisms associated with nosocomial pneumonia depend on the onset of infection. The organisms causing early-onset pneumonia (within 4-5 days of admission) are similar to those of community-associated pneumonia (CAP). Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of CAP. The likelihood that other organisms may be involved depends on the age of the patient and the clinical scenario (previous illness, immunocompromised state, travel history, exposure to animals or contaminated water). It is also associated with early-onset hospital-acquired pneumonia but not late-onset hospital-acquired pneumonia. Option B - Mycoplasma pneumoniae: Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia is common in younger individuals rather than elderly people. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Segmental bronchi: Due to their small overall cross-sectional area, intermediate-sized bronchi, particularly segmental bronchi, are the main causes of airway obstruction. Although there is less airway resistance in a single big airway than in a single small airway, the overall airway resistance is drastically reduced due to the increased cross-sectional area of the numerous parallel pathways. In addition, laminar airflow occurs in tiny passages, further reducing lung resistance. This explains why less than 20% of the overall airway resistance is accounted for by small airways (less than 2 millimetres in diameter). Incorrect Options: Option B - Conducting bronchioles: Despite their big cross-sectional area and high quantity, conducting bronchioles do not make up most of the airway resistance. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Chest Computed Tomography (CT) scan: The patient's clinical presentation and laboratory findings are consistent with Bronchiectasis, a chronic respiratory disease characterized by permanent dilatation and thickening of the bronchial walls. The most appropriate diagnostic test for Bronchiectasis is a chest computed tomography (CT) scan. A Chest Computed Tomography scan is the gold standard diagnostic test for Bronchiectasis. It is the most sensitive and specific test for diagnosing the condition and allows for accurate localization and characterization of bronchial abnormalities. Computed Tomography findings in Bronchiectasis include bronchial wall thickening, cystic changes, signet ring appearance on cross section, and bronchial dilation with visible airway lumen. Computed Tomography can also help identify the underlying cause of Bronchiectasis, such as cystic fibrosis, immune deficiencies, focal obstruction or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Incorrect Options: Option B - Sputum culture and sensitivity: Sputum culture and sensitivity can help identify the causative organism in patients with Bronchiectasis. Sputum culture may be useful in guiding antibiotic therapy in patients with recurrent infections. However, sputum culture and sensitivity alone are not a definitive diagnostic test for Bronchiectasis. It can also be positive in other respiratory conditions, such as pneumonia or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Option C - Pulmonary Function Tests: Pulmonary Function Tests are non-invasive and typically involve a series of breathing tests, including spirometry, lung volume measurements, and diffusing capacity tests Pulmonary Function Tests are not diagnostic for Bronchiectasis, but they can help assess the disease's severity and monitor treatment response. Pulmonary Function Tests may reveal obstructive or restrictive lung patterns, reduced lung volumes, and decreased gas exchange. Option D - Bronchoscopy: During a bronchoscopy, a thin, flexible tube with a camera on its end is inserted through the nose or mouth and into the lungs. The camera allows the doctor to see the inside of the airways and to look for signs of inflammation, blockages, or abnormalities. Bronchoscopy may be useful in identifying endobronchial lesions, such as tumors or foreign bodies, which can cause Bronchiectasis. However, bronchoscopy is not routinely performed in the diagnostic workup of Bronchiectasis and is not the most appropriate initial diagnostic test. @Neet_pg_bot
